common_name: Big Ears Lamb's Ear (Helen von Stein Giant Woolly Betony)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; give this giant-leaved selection extra room since its large rosettes spread wider than the species.

directions: 'Big Ears', also sold as 'Helen von Stein' or 'Helene von Stein', is a giant-leaved lamb's ear selection whose thick, felted silver leaves can reach 8 inches long, roughly double the size of the species and held in a dense, low rosette. Selected for superior heat and humidity tolerance, it rarely if ever sends up the tall woolly flower spikes typical of straight Stachys byzantina, so the silver foliage mat stays clean and unbroken through the growing season. Give it lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; like other lamb's ears it is prone to summer crown rot in wet or humid conditions, so avoid overhead watering and heavy mulch against the crowns. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to refresh vigor and control spread.

common_name: Silver Carpet Lamb's Ear (Non-Flowering Woolly Betony)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; because 'Silver Carpet' is sterile and sets no seed, it must be propagated by division rather than seed.

directions: 'Silver Carpet' is a sterile, essentially non-flowering lamb's ear selected for its dense, low mat of small, intensely silvery, woolly leaves, staying neater and shorter than the species since it rarely sends up flower spikes. Because it sets no seed, all its energy goes into foliage, making it one of the tidiest silver groundcovers for edging paths or lining a dry border. It requires the same lean, sharply drained soil and full sun as other lamb's ears, and is best kept out of high-humidity, poorly drained sites where its dense foliage can trap moisture and rot. Shear off any occasional flower stems and divide crowded mats in spring to maintain the tight, carpet-like habit.

common_name: Cotton Boll Lamb's Ear (Fluffy White-Bracted Woolly Betony)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; 'Cotton Boll' is sterile and propagated only by division.

directions: 'Cotton Boll' is a curious lamb's ear selection whose flowering stems produce dense, fuzzy white bracts that resemble small cotton bolls instead of the usual small lavender flowers, adding an unusual textural accent above the silver woolly foliage mat. Like other named lamb's ear selections it is sterile and does not set seed, so it spreads slowly by rhizome rather than self-sowing around the garden. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since like all Stachys byzantina forms it is prone to crown rot in wet, humid, or heavy clay conditions. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the mat vigorous and tidy.

common_name: Geisha Girl Flowering Quince (Apricot-Pink Double Late-Blooming Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Geisha Girl flowers later than most quince cultivars, extending the flowering quince season into mid-spring.

directions: 'Geisha Girl' is a later-blooming, more compact flowering quince selection bearing semi-double, soft apricot-pink flowers accented by prominent yellow stamens, opening on the bare branches in mid-to-late spring after many other quince cultivars have finished. A UK Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit winner, it forms a dense, rounded, spiny shrub with glossy dark green foliage and small, aromatic yellow-green fruit useful for preserves though too tart to eat fresh. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to avoid removing the next season's buds.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Contorta's slow, compact growth and twisted branch structure make it a good specimen for winter interest near a patio or entry.

directions: 'Contorta' is a slow-growing, compact flowering quince selection prized for its dense, twisted, corkscrew-like dark brown branches, which provide sculptural winter interest long after the leaves have dropped. In early spring, pale peach-pink flowers fading toward white open directly on the contorted stems ahead of the curled, twisted foliage that follows, giving the shrub a strikingly gnarled silhouette all season. Small, fragrant, yellow-green fruit follows the bloom, usable for jelly and preserves. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune, if needed, only right after flowering to preserve next year's buds.
